newsitem.title: USA: Economists rap White House global warming response.
newsitem.headline: Economists rap White House global warming response.

text.p: The Clinton administration appears nearly as pessimistic as fossil fuels industry groups when it comes to assessing the economic impacts of fighting global warming, economists said on Tuesday.

"The Clinton administration has fallen into the same worst-case scenario as industry," Florentin Krause, of the International Project for Sustainable Energy Paths, said at a briefing sponsored by the Environmental Information Center.

The administration, set to release its economic impact analysis on reducing greenhouse gases in June or July, is following the path of industry groups and not taking into account pollution control measures that could have economic offsets or benefits, the economists said.

Fearful of a business backlash, the administration is discussing voluntary programs to reduce pollution when it should be considered big changes in the tax system, taking advantage of the ongoing restructuring of the electric power industry and encouraging technological advances, they said.
"Voluntary programs are good, but they're not going to fix this one," Krause said.

He said the administration should "give up its backward-looking modeling approach," and look at bolder options that include an energy tax offset by some other tax reduction or shift, elimination of subsidies for fossil fuel use, and policies to encourage technology advances.
The White House could use the current interest in restructuring the tax code and in restructuring the electric power industry to develop ways to discourage pollution, the economists said.
For example utilities could be taxed on their emissions instead of their profits, said Bill Moomaw, of the Fletcher School of Diplomacy at Tufts University.
"We're wasting opportunities, in some ways because government is in the way of regulatory change," Moomaw said.

A BTU tax, which Congress rejected early in the Clinton administration, could pass if the administration rallied environmentalists behind it and if there were offsetting tax cuts, said Frank Muller, of Environment Tax Program.

Industry groups charged that reducing emissions of carbon from burning fossil fuels would cost the U.S. economy billions of dollars and put the nation at a huge disadvantage to China, South Korea and other rapidly developing economies that would not be bound by industrialized nations' agreement to reduce pollution.

While stressing that details of the administration's economic anaylsis were not available, Krause said he understood that it took some advantage of gains from more use of renewable fuels, but did not take gains from efficiency improvements very much into account.

The administration proposed using a system of trading allowances to pollute as a way to encourage industries to reduce carbon emissions, but has not proposed emissions caps, a timeframe for reaching goals, or specifics on how reductions would be made.
Industrialized nations are negotiating an agreement to reduce the heat-trapping emissions, and hope to reach a deal in a final meeting in December in Japan.
